title: Lateral Canthotomy & Cantholysis
keywords: this is a clinical diagnosis and a bedside procedure, do not wait for CT or ophthalmology if vision is threatened
cut the lateral canthal tendon first, then the inferior crus, then the superior crus only if pressure remains elevated
strumming the crus with closed scissors to confirm it's fully released, it should feel like a plucked string when intact and go slack once cut
cut inferoposteriorly toward the orbital rim to avoid the lacrimal gland and levator muscle superiorly

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 6), built alongside the ophthalmologic-emergencies reference which covers the orbital compartment syndrome indication for this procedure.
Reformatted for reading on a phone: long paragraphs broken into short paragraphs and lists. Wording and clinical content unchanged.

purpose: Emergent bedside decompression of orbital compartment syndrome (retrobulbar hemorrhage) to relieve pressure on the optic nerve and central retinal artery before permanent vision loss occurs.
entryPrompt: This is a clinical diagnosis — proptosis, a tense/firm orbit, resistance to globe retropulsion, elevated IOP, and vision loss after orbital trauma. If vision is threatened, do NOT wait for CT imaging or ophthalmology to arrive before decompressing.

nodes.body: Proptosis, a tense/firm globe on palpation, resistance to retropulsion, decreased visual acuity, an afferent pupillary defect, and/or elevated intraocular pressure in the setting of orbital trauma (or post-orbital-surgery). This is a clinical diagnosis — the decision to decompress is made at the bedside based on threatened vision, not on imaging.

Explain the procedure if the patient is able to understand (this is uncomfortable but brief).

Inject roughly 2 mL of 1-2% lidocaine WITH epinephrine into the lateral canthus, directing the needle AWAY from the globe — the epinephrine helps with hemostasis in an already-bleeding compartment.

Allow a brief moment for anesthesia to take effect if time allows, but do not delay meaningfully if vision is acutely threatened.

nodes.prompt: 3. Canthotomy — cut the lateral canthal tendon
nodes.body: Using straight iris/tenotomy scissors (or a hemostat first to crush the tissue for a moment to reduce bleeding, if available and time allows), cut from the lateral canthal angle laterally toward the orbital rim, roughly 1-2 cm — this is the canthotomy. You should feel/see the lateral commissure open.

1. Grasp and lift the lateral lower eyelid away from the globe with forceps.
2. With the scissors angled AWAY from the globe, identify the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon — 'strumming' it with closed scissors helps confirm you have it (it feels like plucking a taut string when intact).
3. Cut the inferior crus, directing the cut INFEROPOSTERIORLY toward the orbital rim (this trajectory avoids the lacrimal gland, lacrimal artery, and levator muscle, which sit superiorly).

The lower lid should now move freely, separated from the orbital rim.

nodes.prompt: 5. Reassess — is the pressure adequately relieved?
nodes.body: Recheck intraocular pressure and/or clinical tension of the globe after inferior cantholysis alone — this is sufficient in many cases. If IOP remains significantly elevated (commonly cited threshold: still >40 mmHg) or the globe remains tense, proceed to superior cantholysis.

nodes.prompt: 6. Superior cantholysis (if inferior alone is insufficient)
nodes.body: Retract the upper eyelid to expose the superior crus of the lateral canthal tendon. Identify it the same way (strumming) and cut it with iris scissors, again directing away from the globe, to fully release the lateral canthal attachment and allow maximal globe decompression.

checklist: Orbital compartment syndrome recognized clinically and treated without waiting for CT/ophthalmology if vision is threatened
Local anesthetic with epinephrine injected away from the globe before incision
Canthotomy performed, then inferior cantholysis with the cut directed inferoposteriorly away from the lacrimal gland/levator
IOP/clinical tension reassessed after inferior cantholysis before deciding whether superior cantholysis is needed
Ophthalmology involved emergently regardless of immediate decompression success — this buys time, it is not definitive treatment
